title: Learning to Live with AI: How Students Develop AI Literacy Through Naturalistic ChatGPT Interaction
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students develop AI literacy through everyday, naturalistic use of ChatGPT rather than through formal AI instruction. The core research question is how undergraduate students learn to work productively and critically with generative AI in real academic life, including how they respond to AI errors, limitations, and opportunities. The authors position this as a gap in the literature, arguing that many AI literacy frameworks are normative and describe what students should know, while offering less evidence about how AI literacy actually develops in practice.

The study uses a mixed-methods design centered on real-world ChatGPT interaction logs. The authors analyzed 10,536 ChatGPT messages from 36 undergraduates at a research university in the northeastern United States across roughly one academic year. They first conducted grounded qualitative coding on a subset of 1,882 messages, then used the resulting codebook to scale annotation across the full dataset with GPT-4o, followed by human validation of labels. This process identified five major "use genres" in student-AI interaction: academic workhorse, repair and negotiation, emotional companion, metacognitive partner, and trust calibration.

The population consisted of undergraduate students who exported their complete ChatGPT histories from personal accounts. The context was naturalistic and primarily outside formal classroom intervention, with usage patterns tied to the academic calendar. The setting is best characterized as online, since students interacted with ChatGPT through their own accounts on chat.openai.com over time rather than through a structured instructional program. No teacher-led intervention or training was described.

The main conclusion is that AI literacy emerges as a relational, practice-based competence rather than a one-time skill or purely technical ability. Students developed not only prompt strategies, but also what the authors call repair literacy, emotional regulation practices, and trust calibration skills. The paper argues that students actively negotiate when to rely on, question, repair, or abandon AI outputs, and that these situated practices reveal a more complex form of AI literacy involving technical, emotional, metacognitive, and epistemic dimensions. The authors also conclude that educators should build on these naturally emerging practices when designing AI literacy pedagogy and AI-enabled learning environments.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: A named generative AI conversational assistant from OpenAI used via chat.openai.com for multi-turn natural language interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper analyzes undergraduates' naturalistic year-long interaction logs with ChatGPT to examine how students develop AI literacy through everyday use, including academic task support, emotional support, metacognitive planning, repair during breakdowns, and trust calibration.

findings.finding_summary: Across 10,536 ChatGPT messages from 36 undergraduates over one academic year, qualitative and mixed-methods analysis identified five emergent use genres—academic workhorse, emotional companion, metacognitive partner, repair and negotiation, and trust calibration—interpreted as evidence that students develop AI literacy through naturalistic practice. The authors argue that students built 'genre portfolios' and 'repair literacy' through ongoing interaction rather than formal instruction, but no standardized outcome effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Observed AI literacy practices in exported ChatGPT interaction logs; emergent use genres and repair literacy from qualitative coding and GPT-4o-assisted annotation

findings.finding_summary: Students demonstrated metacognitive regulation and epistemic vigilance in their ChatGPT use, including goal-setting, self-assessment, verification, and strategic decisions about when to trust, repair, or abandon AI outputs. These findings are based on naturalistic log analysis rather than an intervention comparison, so no causal effect estimate was reported.
findings.measure: Metacognitive partner and trust calibration behaviors in interaction logs

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT was frequently used as an 'academic workhorse' for efficient task completion, concept clarification, and code debugging, indicating utility for academic workflow support. At the same time, recurrent breakdowns, factual errors, context-window failures, and prolonged repair sequences showed that usefulness depended on students' repair work and trust calibration; no quantitative efficiency effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Naturalistic task-support, debugging, and repair behaviors in ChatGPT sessions

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods qualitative study using naturalistic logs from 36 students, with validation of coding reliability (Cohen's kappa = 0.75–0.91), but it is not an RCT, QED, or meta-analysis and does not estimate causal effects on learning outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful qualitative evidence of AI literacy development and mixed workflow benefits/limitations, but it does not provide effect sizes or standardized outcome gains, so impact is promising but unclear.
